studies.title: Refuge At Daybreak
studies.meaning: A single request followed by four things it covers, and the list moves from the widest to the most personal. The evil of what He created, which includes everything; then darkness as it settles; then those who blow on knots; then an envier at the moment of envying. The last two are human and near. Each is introduced by the same preposition, so the sentence is one refuge held against four kinds of harm.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by the tradition this collection follows, though some classical authorities place it in Medina. They connect it to an occasion of harm worked against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The reports differ. The surah is the first of the two that close the Quran. Both are cast as instructions to say something rather than as statements.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to split something open. It names dawn as the cracking of the night, and the same root is used of a seed splitting and of the sea parting for Moses.
The first word names night as something that pours in, the second a thing entering and staying. Classical readers also apply it to the moon when it sets, and both readings are recorded.
The clause is timed, not general. What is sought refuge from is not a person of a certain character but a moment, the point at which the envy is active, which is a narrower and fairer thing to name.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night was the dangerous half of the day. Snakes moved, raids came before dawn, and a traveller who had to keep going did it in the dark. Knots were also a practical thing rather than an image: cords were tied with intention, for oaths and for charms, and a knotted cord was a recognised object in that world. Both fears in this surah were ordinary.
studies.didYouKnow: These two closing surahs are known together as the pair of refuge-seekings. A well-known report describes them being recited each night and blown into the hands, which were then passed over the body, beginning with the head. The Quran ends with two chapters about being afraid, and both begin with the word say.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refuge is asked from the Lord of daybreak, and that title is not incidental. The one being asked is named by an act of splitting darkness, so the request is addressed to the very trait that answers it. The list then admits that harm exists inside creation, without explaining why. The surah's answer to that problem is not an argument but a move. You do not remove the danger. You change where you are standing.

crossReferences.why: Completes the pair, turning from external harms to one that works inside the chest.
Uses the same title for God, joining the splitting of dawn to the making of night.
Shows envy handled practically inside a family, by withholding information rather than by confrontation.

studies.applyIt: Say this surah tonight with the last line meant about a specific moment rather than a specific person. Envy is timed in the ayah, not permanent, and that includes your own. If the moment you thought of was yours, that is the more useful reading, and it does not need to be said out loud to anyone.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to say that they take shelter with the Lord of the dawn. They ask him for safety from the harm in what he made. They ask for safety from the dark night, from people who work spells, and from anyone who is jealous.
